title: Multi-Regime Neural ODE For 6D Flight Dynamics

sections.heading: 2.1 Problem Formulation
paragraphs: We investigate the problem of learning a continuous-time dynamics model of a high-performance aircraft from trajectory data across varying environments. Here, the predicted state is represented by
x(t) = [n, e, h, ϕ, θ, ψ, p, q, r, ub, vb, wb]⊤ ∈ R12   (1)
where n, e, h denote inertial position, ϕ, θ, ψ denote Euler attitude angles, p, q, r denote body angular rates, and ub, vb, wb are body frame velocity vectors. The control vector is represented by

which includes the normalized aileron, elevator, rudder, and throttle commands. The body-frame velocity components are included since the aerodynamic response depends on both the speed and direction of the aircraft's motion. We use JSBSim to generate the ground-truth dynamics. The simulator evolves the state according to an ordinary differential equation (ODE):
dx/dt = f(x, u)   (3)

where f combines the rigid-body equations with aerodynamic forces and moments obtained from interpolated lookup tables. Our goal is to approximate f with a neural network fθ so that the trajectories obtained by integrating fθ from an initial state x(0) under a known control sequence u(t) reproduce the same ground-truth trajectories:

This task's central difficulty is that high-performance flight dynamics often exhibit stiff, multi-timescale behavior, posing a challenge for Neural ODE learning. The body angular rates respond to control inputs within fractions of a second. Several aircraft responses occur on relatively short timescales, including short-period, Dutch-roll, and roll-subsidence behavior. The short period and Dutch roll oscillate with periods of roughly one to a few seconds. Roll subsidence damps out over a similar time interval, but it decays instead of oscillating. Meanwhile, position and speed change at a much slower scale, evolving over tens of seconds (phugoid, positional drift). The separation of timescales within a single state vector creates a challenging multi-timescale learning problem for a Neural ODE.
The JSBSim F-15 model is treated as a controlled testbed for learning stiff, multi-timescale 6-DOF dynamics, with the prediction accuracy evaluated relative to the simulator.

sections.heading: 2.2 Simulation Environment
paragraphs: All training and evaluation datasets are generated with JSBSim 1.3.1, an open-source flight dynamics engine, using its bundled F-15 model. JSBSim integrates the full six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) rigid-body equations of motion at its native 120 Hz timestep, with the aerodynamic forces and moments obtained from coefficient lookup tables indexed by angle of attack, Mach number, and control-surface deflections.

JSBSim was chosen over alternatives for a variety of reasons. First, JSBSim is headless and scriptable, allowing programmatic generation of thousands of trajectories that have randomized initial conditions and control inputs. Secondly, its dynamics are transparent. The equations of motion and aerodynamic tables are all inspectable, allowing us to determine the exact validity envelope of the aerodynamic model and enforce it during data generation through per-trajectory guards (Section 2.4). Lastly, JSBSim is a popular, established tool in aerospace simulation and reinforcement-learning literature. Unlike proprietary flight recorder and quick-access recorder (QAR) data used in many prior Neural-ODE flight dynamics work, JSBSim permits full public release of the generation code and data, making the benchmark easily reproducible from fixed random seeds.

The bundled F-15 model used by JSBSim is an approximation constructed from public-domain data. This is sufficient for our purposes since the aircraft serves as a reproducible nonlinear 6-DOF testbed with stiff, multi-timescale behavior. Therefore, all reported model errors are evaluated relative to the trajectories generated by the simulator.

sections.heading: 2.3 Data Generation
paragraphs: Five datasets are generated using an identical trajectory protocol, with each dataset differing in one primary experimental axis relative to the baseline. Dataset A is the subsonic core used for primary single-regime comparison. Dataset B varies the flight regime, pushing the initial conditions into the transonic/supersonic range. Datasets C_high and C_low push the altitude to the high and low envelope edges of the F-15. Dataset D varies the aggressiveness of the maneuvers while staying in Dataset A's flight envelope. All datasets carry per-trajectory regime labels and generation metadata, permitting labeled concatenation at training time without loss of stratification (Table X).

Each dataset consists of 1,000 trajectories. Each trajectory is simulated to be 15 seconds long and recorded at the native 120 Hz timestep. This yields 1,800 samples per run in a 21-column record: time, the 12 predicted flight dynamic states, four auxiliary variables, and the four control inputs. Each trajectory begins with the aircraft initialized in level flight and at a random altitude, Mach number, and heading. The aircraft is then trimmed to a steady-state equilibrium wherever a trim solution exists. In the case of a trim failure, which occurs predominantly at the thin-air envelope edge, the trajectory is retained and marked with a trim-failure flag. These flags are preserved as generation metadata for tracking trim success rates, but are not used to filter training or evaluation. Excitation is then applied as sampled maneuvers, with timing, amplitude, and width drawn independently per trajectory, and the resulting state evolution is recorded. Excitation widths range from 0.3- 1.2 s, corresponding to 9- 36 supervision intervals at the 30 Hz supervision rate, to ensure that control transitions are represented across multiple supervised samples. Engine throttle is fixed at its trim setting and held constant, with both engines running, for the duration of each run. Therefore, thrust-transient dynamics fall outside the scope of the dataset.

Table 1. Stratified Dataset Design. Each dataset varies by one primary experimental axis relative to Dataset A, which acts as a baseline. All five share an identical trajectory pool of 15s at 120 Hz, giving 1800 samples per run.

For datasets A-C, control excitation is designed to reveal the aircraft's characteristic dynamics without leaving the initial operating condition. Control excitation for Datasets A-C appears in the form of doublets. Doublets are a positive deflection held briefly, followed by an equal negative deflection before releasing. It is the standard system identification input in flight testing. They excite the characteristic modes while keeping the aircraft within its trimmed neighborhood. Inputs on the three axes are staggered in time within each trajectory so that each axis's response rings out separately. Dataset A trajectories consequently remain within approximately ±2 g and ≤25° bank, whereas Dataset D extends past these limits and reaches approximately 4.9 g and bank angles beyond 160°.

Dataset D replaces doublets with an aggressive maneuver library. Each trajectory has one maneuver drawn, including sustained pulls, in which the elevator is held for several seconds; wind-up turns, which roll to a bank angle and then sustain a pull; roll captures, which hold large aileron deflections and rotate the aircraft through large bank angles, including past inverted; and multi-axis doublets, which overlap large-amplitude inputs on all axes.

This design separates three distinct sources of difficulty that are often conflated. The first is timescale stiffness, which is present at every operating point and the subject of the core experiment. The second is the regime nonlinearity along the Mach axis, which dataset B is designed to probe as transonic drag rise produces sharp coefficient changes. The third is the state-space nonlinearity from aggressive maneuvers that Dataset D is designed to probe. Keeping these on separately labeled datasets allows the core architecture comparison to be unconfounded.

The evaluation datasets probe three distinct extrapolation axes rather than a single ordering of difficulty. Datasets B and C are environmental extrapolations with their initial-condition boxes lying outside A's in Mach and altitude/air-density, respectively. In contrast, Dataset D shares A's environmental box but is the deepest state-space extrapolation due to its trajectories reaching angles of attack, load factors, and attitudes far beyond anything the training distribution contains. Dataset D is deliberately designed to operate closest to the aerodynamics model's validity boundary. Its angle-of-attack guard is limited to 18°, which is a 2° margin from the narrowest coefficient table's edge of 20°. Dataset D probes the most extreme dynamics the simulator can represent with full fidelity.

sections.heading: 2.4 Fidelity enforcement
paragraphs: Direct inspection of the F-15 aerodynamic tables shows that the narrowest coefficient table has a limited angle of attack range. When this limit is exceeded, JSBSim clamps the lookup to a boundary value, producing plausible-looking but frozen coefficients. To ensure the model stays truthful, we enforce validity during data generation. Dataset D monitors the angle of attack at every timestep and rejects any trajectory exceeding the allowed range of -15° to 18° (providing a 2° margin). This guarantees that no retained sample enters the clamped-table region. Additional guards are put in place to reject any trajectories that contain NaN/Inf values, Dataset A trajectories exceeding Mach 0.92 (preventing transonic effects from entering the subsonic core), Dataset Clow trajectories descending below 200 ft, and Dataset D trajectories descending below 500 ft. No explicit minimum-altitude guard is applied to Datasets A, B, or Chigh because their initial altitude ranges remain well above ground over the 15-second simulation horizon under the relatively mild doublet excitation. To mitigate early configuration errors, we abort generation if more than 30,000 attempts are needed to collect the 1,000 retained trajectories. All datasets use a fixed per-dataset random seed for reproducibility.

sections.heading: 2.5 Preprocessing
paragraphs: The datasets are split 70/15/15 into train/validation/test partitions at the trajectory level with stratification so that each regime contributes 700/150/150 trajectories. We avoid splitting at the timestep level because adjacent 120 Hz samples are nearly identical, which would leak training information into evaluation. We drop the time column and the four auxiliary variables before training, leaving only 12 predicted states and four controls. North and east position remain prediction targets but are removed from the input, leaving ten state inputs and four control inputs. Roll and heading are unwrapped before any derivatives are computed to remove the 2π discontinuities. Without this, the jump from 359° back to 0° registers as an enormous instantaneous yaw rate, which corrupts the finite-difference derivatives of ψ. Features are normalized using z-scores computed from the training partition only, and those statistics are stored for denormalization at evaluation.

Training operates on short windows rather than full trajectories. Each sample is a 3-second (360-step) segment consisting of the initial state, the control sequence over the window, and the target state sequence. During training, states are supervised every fourth simulator sample (90 supervision points per 3-second window). Windows are drawn from random offsets each epoch to provide training samples without increasing storage. Final evaluation uses complete 15-second rollouts at the full 120 Hz resolution to measure the error that compounds over the long rollout horizon. The training-window length is fixed at 3 seconds across all final model comparisons.

Figure 1. Data Generation and preprocessing. Trajectories are generated from randomized initial conditions, checked against aerodynamic feasibility, split by trajectory, normalized using training statistics, and sampled into 3-second training windows.

sections.heading: 2.6 Models
paragraphs: All models share the same interface. They are given an initial state x(0) and the control sequence u(t), and the model produces a predicted trajectory by using numerical integration of a learned vector field.
Figure 2. Neural ODE forward pass. The numerical solver repeatedly queries the learned vector field fθ to advance the predicted state. Each query is counted as one function evaluation.
Controls enter the vector field by piecewise-constant lookup at the solver's query time, matching the zero-order hold used during data generation.

The baseline vector field is a three-hidden-layer multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with 128 nodes per layer and 36,492 parameters. It takes the ten state variables and four control inputs and produces derivatives for all 12 predicted states. A hyperbolic tangent (tanh) is used to provide a smooth learned vector field for numerical integration. The baseline width is fixed at 128 units to provide a compact reference architecture for the controlled comparisons below.

A capacity-control ablation accompanies the baseline model. The same architecture is trained under an identical protocol, but at a substantially increased hidden width of 181 units with 70,783 parameters (twice that of the baseline). Its purpose is to test whether any advantage of the modified model comes from its structure rather than having greater model capacity. The state-scaled model uses the same MLP architecture as the baseline but adds a learnable output scale for each of the 12 derivatives. The scales are stored in logarithmic form so that they remain positive during training.

The multiscale model partitions the state according to a hypothesized fast/slow timescale structure and organizes the learned vector field around that partition. There are two branches, each being a three-hidden-layer MLP of width 89 with tanh activations that receive the full 14-dimensional input. It has a fast branch that outputs the derivatives of attitude (φ, θ, ψ) and body rates (p, q, r). It has a slow branch that outputs the derivatives of position (n, e), altitude (h), and body-frame velocity (ub, vb, wb).

Each of the 12 state derivatives gets its own learnable scale. We store each scale as a logarithm so it stays positive throughout the training. The initial values come from the data. For each state, the finite-difference derivative is taken across the training trajectories and its standard deviation is used to measure how fast that state typically changes. The branches write their outputs back into the standard state ordering, so the output looks identical to the baseline's from the outside. Both branches receive all ten inputs and all four controls. The split shapes what each branch produces, not information flow, since fast and slow dynamics are physically coupled. In total, the multiscale model has 35,802 parameters against the baseline's 36,492, a difference of 1.89%, with per-evaluation multiply-accumulate cost differing by 2.36%. A second multiscale configuration uses the same architecture and parameter count but assigns only the body rates (p, q, r) to the fast branch.

Because the multiscale configuration retains the same learnable per-state derivative scaling used by the state-scaled model, the state-scaled architecture is used to isolate the effect of fast/slow branching. These two configurations differ only in which states are assigned to the fast branch.

Figure 3. Multiscale Vector Field. The fast and slow branches receive the same state-control input but predict different subsets of the state derivatives. The outputs are scaled and reassembled into the full 12-dimensional derivative vector.

For multi-regime training, two conditioned variants of the state-scaled architecture are trained on the combined A, B, Chigh, Clow datasets and receive an additional regime-conditioning signal. No gating network or separate regime experts are used. Instead, the same network is used across all regimes, with the conditioning signal changing how the vector field responds. Two conditioning methods are tested: a learned embedding of the discrete regime label and FiLM modulation. For the control baseline, a state-scaled model trained on the same combined dataset is used. This allows us to test whether explicitly providing regime information improves performance beyond simply training on a wider range of flight conditions.
Figure 4. Multi-Regime Conditioning. Models are trained across datasets A, B, Chigh, Clow, with regime information supplied through either a learned embedding or FiLM modulation.

Dataset D is excluded from the multi-regime training by design for two reasons. First, Dataset D is not a regime. It shares the same environmental box as Dataset A and only differs in maneuver aggressiveness. Therefore, a regime label for D would be uninformative about what distinguishes its trajectories. Conditioning on Dataset D would conflate the maneuver axis with the regime axis, negating the goal of the stratified design. Second, excluding Dataset D from all training preserves it as a pure held-out maneuver-generalization test for every model in the comparison.

sections.heading: 2.7 Numerical Solvers
paragraphs: A Neural ODE produces a trajectory by handing its learned vector field to a numerical solver, which integrates it forward through time. Therefore, every prediction costs many evaluations of fθ. For adaptive solvers, the number of evaluations depends on how difficult the learned dynamics are to integrate. All models are trained using fixed-step fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4). Final evaluation uses full-resolution RK4 with a timestep of (dt = 1/120)s matching the 120 Hz simulator sampling rate.

To test whether the reported architecture comparisons depend on the numerical integration scheme, we perform a post-hoc solver robustness check on the baseline and rates-only multiscale configurations across five paired seeds. The same saved checkpoints are also reevaluated using RK4 at the standard timestep, RK4 with the timestep halved, and the adaptive Dormand-Prince method (DOPRI5). This check is used only to test numerical robustness and is not treated as a separate architecture-solver experiment. Training uses fixed-step RK4 with supervision applied every fourth simulator sample. Gradients are computed by backpropagation through the solver.

sections.heading: 2.8 Training Protocol
paragraphs: All models are trained using Adam with a learning rate of 10-3 and a batch size of 32, on randomly windowed 3-second segments. The optimizer is held fixed across comparisons. Training minimizes mean squared error between the integrated trajectory and the target over supervision points. The loss is computed in normalized coordinates:

Here n indexes the N windows in a batch and m indexes the M supervision points within each window. A 3-second window supervised at every fourth timestep gives M = 90. During training, we supervise every fourth timestep, and during evaluation we use full resolution. Before any comparative experiment, every architecture must pass a single-trajectory overfit test, which requires a normalized rollout RMSE below 0.05 on a single memorized window, to verify the training machinery independently of its learning capacity.

The primary experiment uses five paired random seeds, which control model initialization, training window selection, and data shuffling. As a post-primary robustness extension, the dataset A-trained core models are extended to ten total seeds, while the multi-regime models remain at five seeds. Results are reported using the mean and standard deviation across seeds, and with the individual seed values. Because corresponding configurations use the same random seed, comparisons between the architectures are evaluated using paired statistical tests. Hyperparameters shared across compared models are held constant within any comparison. These include the optimizer, learning rate, batch size, supervision density, and window length. Training uses validation-based early stopping with a minimum of 10 epochs and a patience of 15 epochs. The initial training ceiling was 120 epochs, and runs that reached this ceiling were continued to 160 epochs. The two runs that remained capped were continued to 190 epochs. All final runs ultimately termianted throught he early-stopping criterion rather than a hard epoch ceiling. Hyperparameters and model checkpoints are tuned on the validation partition only, with the test partition reserved for final reported numbers. sections.heading: 2.9 Evaluation Metrics
paragraphs: The main metric is per-timescale normalized RMSE, where rollout error is computed in the z-scored space to make the states comparable. Errors are reported separately for the fast group (p, q, r) and the slow group consisting of the remaining nine predicted states, rather than as a single aggregate.
This separation prevents aggregate metrics from obscuring timescale-specific error.
We report five supporting metrics:
1. Aggregate normalized RMSE for comparability with work that does not separate timescales.
2. Full 15-second rollout RMSE evaluated at the native 120 Hz resolution to measure error accumulation over the complete predicted horizon.
3. Per-state normalized RMSE to identify which individual states drive differences in the fast, slow, and aggregate errors.
4. Regime-stratified evaluation for the multi-regime models, with errors reported separately on each dataset. Dataset D is evaluated separately as a held-out maneuver-generalization test.
5. A post-hoc numerical robustness check comparing the primary evaluation under RK4 at the standard timestep, RK4 with the timestep halved, and DOPRI5.

Architecture comparisons use paired statistical tests across matching random seeds. Effect sizes are reported using paired Cohen's dz. We also report the number of seeds for which each model achieves a lower error. When several related comparisons are tested together, p-values are adjusted using the Holm procedure. To measure uncertainty from the finite test set, we also use paired trajectory-level bootstrapping. Here, whole test trajectories are resampled with replacement, using the same resampled indices for both models. Each regime contains 150 held-out trajectories while using 10,000 bootstrap resamples. For each sample, the rollout RMSE difference is recomputed with a 95% confidence interval.

Figure 5. Evaluation Framework. Models are evaluated using full 15-second rollouts, fast-group, slow-group, aggregate, and per-state normalized RMSE, paired seed-level statistical comparisons, trajectory-level bootstrap confidence intervals, regime-stratified evaluation, and a post-hoc solver robustness check.

sections.heading: 2.10 Experimental Design, comparisons, and ablations
paragraphs: The core of the experiment is a controlled comparison in which exactly one main factor varies per contrast:
[Insert Table]

Table 3. Model Configurations. Each adjacent pair differs by exactly one factor. The table identifies the model labels used throughout the results and the primary factor changed in each controlled comparison. Parameter counts are for the 14-dimensional input and 12-dimensional output.

The experiments trained on Dataset A compare the baseline, capacity-control, state-scaled, and multiscale configurations. The contrast between the baseline and state-scaled model isolates the effect of the learnable per-state output scales. The capacity-control model tests whether any improvement is due to increased model capacity. Because the multiscale models also include the same learnable per-state derivative scaling, the state-scaled model isolates the additional effect of fast and slow branching. The comparison between the baseline and multiscale models compares the standard architecture against explicit fast and slow branching. Lastly, a second multiscale configuration changes only the branch partition, assigning only (p, q, r) to the fast branch to test whether restricting the fast pathway to body angular rates improves the timescale partition.

The multi-regime comparison uses the same combined A, B, Chigh, Clow training data for its three configurations. The state-scaled model is used as an unconditioned control, while the other two models add a learned regime embedding and a FiLM conditioning, respectively. This allows the differences between the three models to be attributed to the conditioning mechanism rather than additional training data.

Each contrast removes or changes a single component while holding the rest fixed, so the design works as a set of ablations without a separate ablation section. The capacity control comparison changes model size, the state-scaled comparison adds per-state output scaling, the state-scaled-to-multiscale comparison adds fast and slow branching, and the partition ablation changes which states are assigned to the fast branch. Dataset D is excluded from all training and is used only as a held-out maneuver-generalization test. The multi-regime comparisons add conditioning. Numerical sensitivity is instead assessed through the post-hoc solver robustness check.

sections.heading: 2.11 Computation and Implementation
paragraphs: All computation and implementation are done using PyTorch with torchdiffeq for differentiable ODE integration. Data generation, preprocessing, correctness tests, and development-scale training on roughly 300-trajectory subsets run on local CPU hardware. These small vector-field networks can be trained in a matter of minutes. Full-scale experiments and training are run on a rented single-GPU instance, an NVIDIA RTX 5090 with 32 GB of VRAM. These include the full multi-seed architecture comparisons, multi-regime training, and final rollout evaluations on the complete datasets. Each processed dataset is roughly 100 to 150 MB, small enough to fit in memory without streaming or sharding. GPU memory is consumed by solver depth and batch size rather than by dataset size.
